articles.title: Ohio wants to add 118 acres around a rare wetland to a nature preserve; if funding comes through, the protected habitat could grow to 450 acres and the family has offered to donate its house and 3 more acres
articles.summary: US News: A conservation effort in Ross County, Ohio, could significantly expand protection around a rare wetland complex if funding is secured for a proposed 1.
articles.body: A conservation effort in Ross County, Ohio, could significantly expand protection around a rare wetland complex if funding is secured for a proposed 118-acre land acquisition. The Ross County Park District is seeking to acquire the property, which would provide a buffer around the Kinnikinnick Fen and Herron Downs nature preserve properties as well as Kinnikinnick Creek. According to the Scioto Valley Guardian, which obtained the information from the Ross County Board of Commissioners, Ross County commissioners voted on September 8 to formally support the acquisition. If the project receives funding through Ohio’s Clean Ohio program, the preserved habitat could eventually grow to an estimated 450 acres. The property’s owners have also offered to donate their house and about three surrounding acres to the park district.Proposed acquisition would expand wetland protectionThe proposed acquisition would add 118 acres to the conservation landscape surrounding the existing Kinnikinnick Fen and Herron Downs properties. Rather than simply adding another isolated parcel of protected land, the acquisition would create a larger buffer around the wetland areas and Kinnikinnick Creek. That additional land could be important because wetlands are closely connected to the surrounding landscape. Water movement through adjoining properties can influence the condition of a wetland, while vegetation around waterways can provide additional protection for habitats and help maintain the character of the broader ecosystem.An initial environmental assessment of the property found a significant water flow path that feeds the wetland at Herron Downs. That finding has added to the conservation value of the proposed acquisition, as protecting the land around a wetland can also help safeguard the natural processes that support it. If funding is approved, the Ross County Park District would acquire the property and add it to the protected landscape.Funding remains key to the expansionThe proposed purchase is dependent on receiving financial support through Ohio’s Clean Ohio program. The county commissioners’ formal endorsement is intended to support the park district’s application as it seeks funding for the acquisition. The project would expand a conservation area that already includes the Kinnikinnick Fen and Herron Downs nature preserve properties. With the additional 118 acres, the total preserved habitat could reach approximately 450 acres.For the park district, the acquisition would therefore represent more than the preservation of a single parcel. It would strengthen the larger conservation area around the wetlands and creek while helping protect land connected to the existing natural areas. The environmental assessment’s identification of a significant water flow path is particularly relevant because changes to land surrounding wetlands can affect water movement and habitat conditions. Protecting the property could help maintain those connections over the long term.Family offers additional land and houseThe property also comes with an unusual offer from the Herron family. If the acquisition moves forward with Clean Ohio funding, the family has offered to donate the house located on the property, along with approximately three acres surrounding it, to the Ross County Park District. That means the conservation effort could ultimately involve more than the 118-acre acquisition itself. The additional three-acre donation would become part of the park district’s holdings, while the house would also be transferred to the organisation.The offer reflects the family’s willingness to support the broader conservation effort while allowing the property to become part of a larger protected landscape. The house and surrounding acreage would also become part of the park district’s holdings, although the immediate focus remains on securing funding for the proposed acquisition.Protecting a connected wetland landscapeThe planned expansion highlights why conservation groups often seek to protect land surrounding sensitive habitats rather than focusing only on the central wetland itself. Wetlands depend on surrounding hydrology, vegetation and drainage patterns. A property that contains a water flow path feeding an existing wetland can therefore have conservation value even when it is not itself entirely covered by wetland habitat.In this case, the proposed 118 acres would provide a buffer between the existing protected areas and surrounding land. Protecting that buffer could help maintain the ecological setting around Kinnikinnick Fen, Herron Downs and Kinnikinnick Creek. The potential 450-acre protected landscape would also create a larger area for conservation. Such additions can make it easier for land managers to protect habitats as a connected system rather than managing individual parcels separately.A larger conservation opportunity for Ross CountyThe commissioners’ support is an important step, but the expansion is not yet guaranteed. The Ross County Park District must still secure funding through the Clean Ohio program before the proposed acquisition can proceed. If that funding comes through, the project would give the county a significantly larger protected wetland landscape while adding another layer of protection around Kinnikinnick Creek and the water system feeding Herron Downs.The Herron family’s offer to donate the house and three additional acres would further strengthen the project. Together, the proposed acquisition and donation could turn the 118-acre property into an important addition to the region’s conservation network. For Ross County, the effort is ultimately about protecting more than a rare wetland itself. By securing the surrounding land and the water pathway connected to it, officials and the park district are seeking to expand protection around the wetland.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Such gimmicks are nothing new’: India slams Pakistan over 'phoney announcement' of Rs 70 lakh bounty on Masood Azhar
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: India on Tuesday criticised Pakistan over its announcement of a PKR 70 lakh reward for information leading to the arrest or conviction of J.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India on Tuesday criticised Pakistan over its announcement of a PKR 70 lakh reward for information leading to the arrest or conviction of Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) chief Masood Azhar, calling it a “phoney” move and asking Islamabad to take concrete action against the terror group chief.Responding to Pakistan maintaining the bounty on Azhar, ministry of external affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said Islamabad's announcement was unlikely to have any consequence."Such gimmicks and attempts at hoodwinking people by Pakistan are nothing new. We have seen similar gimmicks in the past as well. For a state sponsor of terrorism to make such phoney announcements—we all know how hollow they are. Pakistan must take concrete action rather than make announcements that are ultimately of no consequence..."Pakistan has continued to list Azhar in the Federal Investigation Agency's (FIA) “Red Book” of most-wanted terrorists and has retained a reward of PKR 70 Lakh for information leading to his apprehension or conviction.Azhar, the founder and chief of JeM, is wanted in India in connection with several terror cases, including the 2001 Parliament attack. India has also linked JeM to the 2016 Pathankot airbase attack and the 2019 Pulwama bombing.His name was first included in the FIA's Red Book in 2021 and has been retained in its 2026 edition. He is listed at serial number 1480 among 1,804 most-wanted terrorists.The FIA entry identifies Azhar as the head of Jaish-e-Mohammad and says the reward of up to PKR 70 lakh is for information leading directly to his “apprehension or conviction”.The cases cited against him in the FIA list were registered in Gujranwala, Multan and Lahore under provisions of Pakistan's Anti-Terrorism Act.India has for years accused Pakistan of sheltering Azhar. Islamabad has maintained that he fled to Afghanistan, a claim rejected by Afghanistan's Taliban government.Azhar was among the fugitives India sought from Pakistan following the 2008 Mumbai terror attacks, in which 10 Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorists killed 166 people.The latest development comes ahead of the Financial Action Task Force's next plenary in Paris from October 26 to 30. Pakistan was placed on the FATF's increased monitoring list, commonly known as the grey list, in 2018 and remained there until 2022.It was removed after completing commitments under two FATF action plans focused on strengthening its anti-money laundering and counter-terror financing framework and implementing targeted financial sanctions.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine will pause attacks if Russia spares infrastructure
articles.summary: Zelenskyy insists de-escalation depends on US ensuring Russia’s genuine readiness to stop war and attacks on Ukraine.
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine is ready to halt its attacks on Russian territory if the United States can secure a commitment from Russia to not hit Ukrainian infrastructure.

Zelenskyy’s comments came on Monday after US President Donald Trump claimed that Ukraine and Russia decided to stop targeting each other’s energy sites, without providing details.

Trump’s message came a day after he said that rising diesel prices around the world are “mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine war” and “not Iran” , in a statement on Truth Social.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s halting of attacks would be dependent on the US ensuring that Russia is “genuinely ready to stop this war aimed at destroying life, and to do so for real and for the long term”. Only then would Ukraine take “de-escalatory steps”, he added.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine had proposed that its partners secure an agreement with Russia to halt attacks on critical infrastructure, accusing Moscow of targeting food, energy and other basic facilities “that sustain life”.

Russia’s repeated attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure have put a strain on fuel systems necessary for heating and electricity, leading to fears that civilians could face a difficult winter.

“These systems are vulnerable and Russia has been using this vulnerability, leaving thousands of households without electricity or heating for the past three winters,” explained Al Jazeera correspondent Dmitry Medvedenko from Moscow.

Ukraine has in recent months demonstrated its growing long-range strike capability, targeting Russian energy infrastructure far from the front lines.

“Ukraine might start responding in kind by hitting essential energy systems, and surely the Kremlin understands there’s a ticking clock for both sides to come to some kind of consensus for this winter to ensure that their populations will be kept warm and with electricity,” Medvedenko added.

The two warring sides continued to exchange air attacks early on Tuesday, with Russian strikes on Kyiv killing one person and wounding seven since the start of the day, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said.

Another two people were killed in separate Russian attacks in the Ukrainian cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, it said.

Elsewhere, Russian forces shot down 222 Ukrainian drones overnight, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said.

Ukraine attacked an industrial facility in Russia with drones overnight, damaging the site and several residential buildings in the southeastern Samara region, Russian media reported.

About 40 drones were shot down, Russian state news agency TASS reported on Tuesday, citing Regional Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev.

Ukrainian media said the targeted industrial facility was an oil refinery.

A “massive” Ukrainian drone attack sparked several fires in the Russian city of Taganrog, regional Governor Yury Slyusar said. He said on Telegram that two apartment buildings and three private homes had been damaged, as well as an educational institution, agricultural warehouses and a site belonging to Russian e-retailer Ozon.

Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that Kyiv’s forces had targeted a drone production facility in the city.

articles.title: Unions warn against 'out of control' political spending
articles.summary: In a joint statement, unions say donations totalling £72m to Reform UK threaten the "integrity of democracy".
articles.body:
Trade unions have called for "out of control" political spending to be reined in, suggesting that the "health and integrity of democracy" have been threatened by donations totalling £72m to Reform UK.

In a joint statement, the TUC - the umbrella group for unions in the UK - called on the government to "protect our democracy from being captured by the super rich".

There is no explicit call for a cap on domestic donations to match those the government plans to impose on foreign-based donations.

But unions have signalled they are open to discussions with policymakers on any initiatives to "clean up" party funding.

The statement, issued at the TUC's annual congress in Brighton, also makes the case that trade union donations should not be treated in the same way as big contributions to parties from rich individuals.

The debate over donations to political parties has been reignited after Reform UK received two donations totalling £72m from two British crypto-billionaires who have both recently lived abroad.

The government is planning to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British voters living overseas, including a £100,000 cap backdated to 25 March.

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.

Since 2020, Labour has received almost £43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees.

Political donors could face tougher residency rules

Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

Many in the trade union movement - especially those with links to Labour - have been wary of a cap on domestic donations in case a future government used this to restrict their donations.

But behind the scenes officials recognise the eye-watering donations from Reform UK have changed the game and some form of domestic cap may have to be considered.

The leader of the Unite union Sharon Graham told the BBC she favoured a cap of £500,000 to £1m on individual donations from UK-based citizens.

But she argued that as union donations are made of lots of individual members making a contribution through a political levy then this should be treated differently.

She said: "There is a difference between a crypto-billionaire based in the UK or abroad giving millions and trade union members who are nurses, cleaners, bus drivers giving 10p a week which adds up cumulatively to what we give to Labour."

The GMB union has been one of the most wary over the implications of a domestic donations cap.

Its general secretary Gary Smith told the BBC: "Whether there will be a cap on political donations, we will wait and see.

"We will talk to the government at the appropriate time but we can't have any confusion between the political voice working people have through their unions and crypto-billionaires."

What is interesting about Tuesday's union statement is not just what it says but what it doesn't.

There has been no consensus on calling for caps on the spending of political parties rather than donations - one option for dealing with the Reform war chest.

Another option was to treat big unions donations as a series of donations from individual members. For example a million strong union that donates £1m to Labour would have been regarded as making donations of £1 a member - thus escaping a cap. Some believe this would be politically difficult to argue.

Not all unions donate to Labour and those which do not are therefore very relaxed about a cap.

One even said the events of the past few days have been helpful in arguing for more restrictions on political donations.

But I understand discussions will continue amongst those unions with financial links to Labour - including the three biggest in the UK - to try to reach a common position on Wednesday behind closed doors in Brighton and possibly in days and weeks ahead.

articles.title: Thousands flee to Djibouti amid renewed Yemen fighting
articles.summary: More than 3,400 people arrived in 48 hours as Djibouti prepares for more.
articles.body:
More than 3,400 people fleeing renewed fighting in Yemen have landed along Djibouti’s northern coast, according to Djiboutian authorities.

The figure was reported by Djibouti’s state news agency on Sunday. It covers just 48 hours of arrivals, part of a surge that Djiboutian officials say began the previous weekend.

The crossings followed a Houthi offensive in which the group, which controls much of northern Yemen, seized the Red Sea port of Mocha and advanced along the coast towards the narrow strait separating Yemen from Djibouti.

Djibouti has fewer than 1.2 million people and limited resources. The arrival of thousands of people within days is putting further strain on already stretched services, officials have warned.

Footage aired on Djibouti’s state broadcaster RTD showed wooden dhows and larger vessels arriving near the town of Obock, crowded with women in black robes and children wearing life jackets.

Obock lies on Djibouti’s northern coast, close to the narrowest stretch of the Bab al-Mandeb between the Horn of Africa and Yemen. The area is near a departure point for refugees making the journey in the opposite direction, through Yemen towards the Gulf.

Those coming ashore could be seen carrying the belongings they had with them, including sacks of clothing, water containers, food and other personal items. In footage filmed after dark, soldiers unloaded the boats under floodlights.

People have arrived on “all kinds of sea vessels, from small dhows to larger ships”, Alexandre Coissac, who heads the International Organization for Migration (IOM) in Djibouti, told Al Jazeera. One vessel alone carried hundreds of people recently, he said.

The journey has also become increasingly difficult, Coissac said, with some families stranded on the Yemeni side due to fuel shortages.

UNICEF said children making the crossing were exposed to extreme heat, dehydration and a lack of safe drinking water.

The IOM said on Sunday that fighting had driven residents out of entire districts in Yemen, including Maqbanah and Jabal Habashi. It put the wider displacement inside Yemen at more than 85,000 people, most of it in just the first two weeks of September.

After Houthi forces seized the strategic Yemeni island of Mayyun, also known as Perim, in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, Djibouti’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on September 11 it was following developments there “with increased attention”, while backing efforts to ease tensions and reach a political solution in Yemen.

Djibouti’s Finance Minister Ilyas Dawaleh documented the accelerating arrivals in a series of posts on X, reporting about 500 people by September 11, 1,400 the following day and more than 2,000 by that evening.

By September 13, he wrote that the pace was becoming “increasingly difficult for our country”.

As arrivals increased, Djibouti’s coastguard, navy, army and health services were deployed to rescue people stranded at sea and receive them ashore, providing food and first aid at sites including Obock and the smaller coastal post of Khor Angar.

On Sunday, Prime Minister Abdoulkader Kamil Mohamed travelled to Obock to meet officials from the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), the World Food Programme and the IOM.

Djiboutian authorities said they were preparing to receive as many as 10,000 people if the pace continued.

The pressure on Djibouti also has implications beyond the humanitarian response. The Bab al-Mandeb is one of the world’s most important shipping corridors, with an estimated one in eight tonnes of global seaborne trade passing through it each day.

Djibouti’s location has also made it a hub for foreign militaries. The United States, China, France, Japan and Italy all operate bases in the country, several within a few miles of one another, in part because of the importance of protecting shipping through the increasingly contested waterway.

“Djibouti, like many countries, depends heavily on international trade and the safety and security of sea lanes,” said Aden Omar Abdillahi, director of the Djibouti-based Institute of Political and Strategic Studies.

“If this conflict impacts maritime security in the way some fear, it will have a massive impact.”

Djibouti has spent two decades building its role as a stable base for foreign governments and shipping interests in an unstable region. The latest crisis puts further pressure on that role as instability around the Red Sea deepens.

In a separate post on X, Dawaleh warned that the US-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted traffic through the critical Strait of Hormuz waterway, is already deepening uncertainty for smaller economies such as Djibouti’s.

In 2015, more than 15,700 Yemenis arrived after the war escalated, according to IOM and Djiboutian government figures.

“We’ve received refugees for decades from across the region,” Abdillahi said.

“When it comes to Yemen, many people settled here during the first big phase of the fighting in 2015, and we’ve got experience managing this. Yemenis are also not distant foreigners; there are Yemeni communities who have been here for centuries.”

Djibouti already hosts more than 36,000 registered refugees and asylum seekers, according to UNHCR’s March figures. Most are from Somalia, Ethiopia and Yemen.

The Markazi camp near Obock, which received thousands of Yemenis during the earlier exodus a decade ago, is again being used to accommodate new arrivals.

“It is at this site that we’re trying to organise and that the authorities are trying to organise all the support in terms of housing, shelter and meals,” IOM’s Coissac told Al Jazeera.

He added that many of the latest arrivals were being accommodated there, while others had been taken in by residents of Obock. “The generosity of the Obock population has been huge,” Coissac said.

In a post on X on September 12, Dawaleh wrote that the UNHCR and other UN agencies on the ground “appear to be lacking resources to receive and protect these vulnerable people with dignity”, and urged the international community to “stand with us urgently”.

A person familiar with the humanitarian response in the region said authorities in Puntland and Somaliland, two self-governing regions of Somalia across the Gulf of Aden, had already asked UN agencies for help preparing for larger numbers.

They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the matter publicly.

Both regions could see arrivals at their own port towns, Bosaso and Berbera, if the exodus continues.

The preparations come as humanitarian organisations are already facing deep funding pressures following sharp reductions in aid from the United States and, more recently, the United Kingdom.

Coissac said many of those arriving were likely to remain in Djibouti rather than move on quickly. “The number of people arriving is large,” he said, “and if it continues at this rate, we’ll not be able to manage”.

articles.title: Bangladesh's banana farmers once discarded the stems; the waste can now produce 37,778 tonnes of fibre a year and a $94 million export opportunity
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Bangladesh’s banana farmers could turn discarded banana stems into a source of income, as researchers estimate the waste could produce nearly 37,778 t.
articles.body: Bangladesh’s banana farmers could turn discarded banana stems into a source of income, as researchers estimate the waste could produce nearly 37,778 tonnes of banana fibre each year, creating a potential $94 million export opportunity. According to the study published in the Journal of Hunan University, titled ‘Unlocking the Potential of Banana Fibre Exports from Bangladesh: A Comprehensive Marketing Strategy Analysis’, the country’s extensive banana cultivation leaves large quantities of pseudo-stems largely unused, even though they can be processed into fibre for textiles, packaging and paper. With global demand for sustainable materials growing, banana fibre could offer Bangladesh a new export product while creating employment in rural areas. But reaching this potential will require investment in processing, quality control, research and international marketing.Banana waste offers Bangladesh a $94 million export opportunityThe fibre estimate becomes particularly significant when its potential export value is considered. The study’s findings state that Bangladesh could earn “over $94 million annually” by exporting banana fibre at a price of $2.50 per kilogram. At the study’s estimated production of 37,778 tonnes, that price works out to about $94.4 million in potential annual revenue, which is why the opportunity can be rounded to $94 million.The researchers are careful to present this as potential rather than money Bangladesh is already earning from banana fibre exports. Their conclusion says the country is “capable of producing approximately 37,778 tons of banana fibre each year from banana plant waste”, with export potential based on production capacity and an export price of $2.50 per kilogram. Existing Bangladeshi exporters operate on a much smaller scale, meaning substantial expansion would be required before the estimated opportunity could become actual export revenue.Banana fibre can be used in many productsBanana fibre’s appeal comes not only from the quantity of available waste but also from the range of products it can be used to make. The study describes banana fibre as a biodegradable natural material composed primarily of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin. It says fibres from different parts of the pseudo-stem can have different characteristics, with inner sheaths producing softer fibres and outer sheaths producing thicker, more robust material.Banana fibre can be used in textiles, packaging and pulp and paper, as well as for products including yarn, fabric, apparel, handicrafts, paper, security-printing materials and plywood. The researchers also point to its strength, moisture absorption and breathability as characteristics that could make it suitable for apparel, home furnishings and technical textiles.Bangladesh needs investment to expand banana fibre exportsBangladesh already has some foundations for a banana fibre trade. The study identifies companies including Musa Banana Fibre and Modern Banana Fibre Company Ltd among the country’s manufacturers and exporters, with existing markets in Eastern Europe, South America, Oceania and Central America. However, the researchers say Bangladesh is “not currently able to export large volumes of banana fibres”, highlighting the gap between the country’s theoretical production potential and its present export capacity.Closing that gap would require investment in machinery, extraction technology, quality control, worker training, transport and storage, alongside stronger international marketing. The study recommends finding new overseas buyers, appointing agents in target markets, investing in research and development and building closer relationships with customers. It also calls for internationally recognised quality standards and says government support through measures such as subsidies, tax incentives and export-promotion schemes could help the industry develop.Banana waste could create rural jobsThey argue that using discarded pseudo-stems could help Bangladesh diversify its export basket, create rural employment and participate in the growing market for sustainable materials. Their study estimates that the global banana fibre market grew at a 5% compound annual growth rate from 2019 to 2023, while stressing that Bangladesh’s $94 million opportunity depends on developing the production, processing, quality and export infrastructure needed to turn agricultural waste into a commercially viable fibre industry.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Israel and Saudi Arabia have held talks mediated by the US Central Command aimed at helping Riyadh defend itself against Houthi attacks through intelligence assistance, as cited by The Jerusalem Post.According to sources cited by JP, the Saudi request for assistance was likely focused on intelligence support to develop a broader picture of Houthi military deployments in the area and identify potential plans for future operations.The Israeli military has already demonstrated intelligence and operational capabilities in the maritime arena around the Strait of Hormuz, assisting the US in building intelligence on the locations of Iranian forces, the sources said.Separately, Bloomberg reported that Saudi Arabia had also requested British assistance to repel the Houthis from the Bab al-Mandab Strait and help defend its oil infrastructure against attacks.Burnham has agreed to send British military advisers to assist Saudi Arabia, Bloomberg reported, but had not yet committed to providing any additional aid.Also read | Pakistan blinks on Houthis, walks back Saudi defence warning within 24 hoursPakistan does not put boots on the groundThe developments have also revived attention on the mutual-defence pact signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on August 7. While the Mecca pact commits the three countries to a collective response in the event of an attack, Pakistan is not preparing to deploy troops on the ground at this stage.Under the agreement, an armed attack against any one of the three countries would be treated as an attack against all, with the pact also providing for closer defence cooperation.Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif said on Wednesday that there should be no ambiguity over the commitment under the agreement. He said the pact’s collective-defence provisions could be activated in the event of an unprovoked attack on any member or if the conflict in Yemen spills over into Saudi Arabia.However, Pakistan’s foreign ministry later clarified that no military response under the agreement was currently under discussion.Tensions escalate in the Middle EastThe Houthi military has intensified its attacks against Saudi Arabia over the past week, including a drone strike on oil pipelines and pumping facilities that partially disrupted operations along the main pipeline.The Houthis also attacked Saudi civilians inside a mosque and nearby buildings close to the Yemen-Saudi Arabia border. Yemeni officials said the group launched a fresh wave of attacks on Saudi territory while reinforcing positions along Yemen’s western coast on the Red Sea, as Saudi Arabia held urgent discussions in Riyadh on how to respond to the advances.Meanwhile, Gulf Arab states postponed planned talks with Iran, raising concerns that the conflict could widen and threaten global oil supplies.The Houthis have also seized several strategically located islands in the Red Sea and prevented Saudi vessels from passing through the Bab al-Mandab Strait.Saudi authorities issued emergency alerts in the affected area and three other southern cities, while 13 civilians were wounded in the Houthi attacks, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said.The Houthi advances in recent days, including the capture of Perim Island at the mouth of the Red Sea, have added pressure on Saudi Arabia’s oil exports after an aerial attack on Thursday forced the shutdown of its east-west pipeline. Riyadh blamed the pipeline attack on Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.Saudi Arabia built the 1,200-kilometre (745-mile) pipeline across the country from the Gulf to the Red Sea in the 1980s to provide an alternative route for oil exports and bypass the Strait of Hormuz, amid threats to the waterway during the Iran-Iraq war.Traders said a prolonged shutdown of the pipeline could cut off as much as 4% of global oil supplies while the Strait of Hormuz remains largely blockaded. articles.title: NATO jets shoot down drone in Lithuanian airspace as Russia grows 'increasingly reckless,' Rutte says
articles.summary: Two Italian Eurofighter Typhoons scrambled under NATO command and downed a drone over Lithuania that officials say likely came from Belarus.
articles.body: Two Italian Eurofighter Typhoons operating under NATO command scrambled overnight and shot down a drone over Lithuania, marking the first time a drone has been downed in the Baltic nation's airspace, officials said Tuesday. The incident came less than a day after NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte warned that strikes close to alliance territory would drive the 32-nation bloc to increase its support for Ukraine. The drone was destroyed near the village of Pratkūnai, about 60 miles northwest of the capital, Vilnius. RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS "Last night, two Italian Eurofighters deployed on NATO Air Defence mission at Siauliai, scrambled and shot down a drone over Lithuanian airspace," a NATO official told Fox News Digital. "The operation was coordinated through NATO’s Combined Air Operations Centre in Uedem, Germany. Investigations are ongoing together with national authorities." Lithuanian officials said the drone most likely entered from neighboring Belarus and remained in the country's airspace for about 30 minutes before it was intercepted. Lithuanian Air Force Commander Antanas Matutis said the recovered drone was "likely" carrying explosives. Authorities are examining the wreckage of the downed drone to determine its origin and purpose. The incident comes amid heightened tensions along NATO's eastern flank. "Russia is growing increasingly reckless as it continues its terrible war against Ukraine," Rutte said, while pledging to strengthen NATO defenses along its eastern flank. In a separate incident Tuesday, Denmark said a Russian frigate fired flares toward a Danish military helicopter conducting routine surveillance over the Baltic Sea. Denmark summoned the Russian ambassador over the encounter. Meanwhile, Russia continued drone strikes across Ukraine, killing three people in Kyiv, Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, according to Ukrainian officials. articles.title: Isle of Man's record summer heatwave in full detail
articles.summary: Isle of Man had its warmest summer on record in 2026, beating the mark set just last year.
articles.body:
The Isle of Man has recorded its warmest summer since records began, according to the government's seasonal climate summary.

Summer 2026 had an average temperature of 16.4C (61.5F), beating the previous record of 16.0C (60.8F), which was set only last year.

It means the island has now had its two warmest summers on record in consecutive years.

The season was also unusually dry and sunny, including a 24-day drought in July and the second-sunniest July ever recorded.

The summer's warmth came from persistently above-average temperatures, rather than any single heatwave.

The average minimum night-time temperature was 13.4C (56.1F), the highest on record, while the mean maximum of 19.4C (66.9F) was the second highest, behind only 1995.

Despite that, the summer's hottest day only reached 27.6C (81.7F), some way short of the all-time record of 28.9C (84F) set in 1983.

There were 34 days of 20C (68F) or higher, the joint second-highest count on record.

June was wetter than average, with 95.8mm of rain falling over the month.

July then turned almost bone dry, with just 2mm falling all month, including a 24-day dry spell from 1 to the 25 July, the fourth-longest drought recorded in any Manx summer.

The total amount of sunshine recorded was 664.8 hours, driven largely by a sunny July. Despite this, it fell well short of the all-time summer sunshine record of 756.7 hours, set in 1995.

Summer 2026 continues a recent run of exceptionally warm seasons on the island.

Alongside 2025, summers in 2018, 2022 and 2023 also rank among the five warmest ever recorded, with records dating back to 1947.

articles.title: Coalition talks likely as no party dominates Philippines’ Bangsamoro region
articles.summary: With 98.56 percent of party-list votes counted, no party has received a majority, according to unofficial results.
articles.body:
Unofficial election results in the Muslim-majority autonomous region of Bangsamoro in the southern Philippines suggest no single party is on course to dominate parliament, meaning that coalition talks may be needed to choose the region’s first chief minister.

The election has been largely shaped by rival camps within the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), a former separatist movement that negotiated autonomy with the Philippine government.

One camp, the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP), is led by longtime Front chairman Al Haj Murad Ebrahim, while the other, the Bangsamoro Federalist Party, is led by Abdulraof Macacua, a former Front commander appointed interim chief by Philippine President Marcos Jr in 2025.

According to partial and unofficial results from the Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting, a church-backed election watchdog, 98.56 percent of the party-list votes have been counted so far.

According to the unofficial results, Macacua’s camp is leading the vote with 35.2 percent, ahead of Murad’s bloc at 32.4 percent.

The BARMM Grand Coalition, the third party on the ballot, has gained 20.5 percent of the vote so far and could emerge as a key player in balancing power in coalition negotiations.

Reporting from Marawi in the southern Philippines, Al Jazeera’s Barnaby Lo said the unofficial results suggest a hung parliament is likely.

“The parties will now have to negotiate to form a coalition government in order to move forward,” Lo said.

According to election officials, the election turnout was about 80 percent, with about 1.8 million votes cast from 2.39 million registered voters.

Voters are electing party, district and sectoral representatives who will form the 80-member parliament tasked with selecting the region’s first elected chief minister, in a vote widely viewed as the most significant milestone since a 2014 peace agreement between Manila and the Front.

articles.title: Who is Lucy Letby? British nurse convicted of killing 7 babies, inquiry finds hospital failures cost lives
articles.summary: UK News: The inquiry into Lucy Letby's murders reveals shocking hospital failures that could have saved lives. Explore the details of her crimes and the ongoing investigation.
articles.body: A public inquiry has found that more babies could have been saved from nurse Lucy Letby if hospital managers had acted sooner on concerns about a rise in unexplained deaths and collapses on a neonatal unit in northern England.The finding came on Tuesday from the Thirlwall Inquiry, which examined how Letby's offending went undetected at the Countess of Chester Hospital and how the hospital responded to concerns about her.Who is Lucy Letby?Letby was born in Hereford, central England, and trained as a nurse at the University of Chester. After qualifying, she began working in the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital.She is serving a life sentence after being convicted of murdering seven newborn babies and attempting to murder eight others while working at the hospital between 2015 and 2016.What the inquiry foundInquiry chair Kathryn Thirlwall described the hospital's failure to protect babies a “complete failure”. She concluded that some of the deaths could have been prevented had concerns about Letby been acted on earlier.The inquiry was not tasked with deciding whether Letby was guilty. Its focus was on how the hospital responded as doctors became increasingly concerned about an unusual pattern of deaths and serious collapses among babies in the neonatal unit.Over 18 months from January 2015, the number of babies dying or suffering unexpected medical collapses increased significantly. Senior doctors raised concerns after several babies suddenly deteriorated and failed to respond to resuscitation as expected.Those concerns eventually led investigators to focus on Letby, who was working on the unit when many of the incidents occurred.What Letby was convicted ofProsecutors argued that Letby deliberately harmed babies by injecting air into their bloodstreams or stomachs, administering excessive amounts of milk or, in some cases, using insulin.The victims included twins and triplets. One set of siblings died on consecutive days, while the youngest baby Letby was convicted of murdering was just one day old.Letby was arrested in 2018 and again in 2019 and 2020 before being charged with the murders and attempted murders.In August 2023, she was convicted of seven murders and seven attempted murders. She was acquitted of two other attempted murder charges, while jurors could not reach verdicts on six alleged attacks.She was convicted in a retrial the following year of attempting to murder another newborn.Letby has consistently denied harming any of the babies and has maintained that she is innocent.Why her convictions remain disputedDespite her convictions, questions about the evidence used against Letby have continued to fuel a campaign arguing that she was wrongly convicted.Some medical specialists have challenged aspects of the prosecution's case. Neonatal doctor Professor Shoo Lee has said research associated with him was misused during Letby's trial and that he and other international experts did not believe the babies had been deliberately attacked.Those challenging the convictions have argued that medical errors and failures at the hospital could have contributed to the babies' deaths and collapses.Letby has made several attempts to appeal her convictions, but the courts have rejected them. Her case has now been referred to the Criminal Cases Review Commission, which is examining whether the convictions are safe. There is currently no timetable for its decision.Police investigation continuesPolice have also examined whether other babies may have been harmed during Letby's time at the Countess of Chester Hospital and during her training at Liverpool Women's Hospital.Prosecutors said in January that no further charges would be brought against Letby. Police described the decision as disappointing.A separate investigation into the hospital's management remains ongoing. Three senior members of the hospital leadership team were arrested last July on suspicion of gross negligence manslaughter.Letby remains in prison serving her life sentence while the Criminal Cases Review Commission considers her case.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Turkish authorities detain at least 150 at protest over LGBTQ+ arrests
articles.summary: Turkish authorities detained at least 150 people on Tuesday after police intervened at a gathering outside Istanbul’s Caglayan courthouse, where demonstrators had planned to protest about recent detentions targeting LGBTQ+ groups, witnesses said.
articles.body: Turkish authorities detained at least 150 people on Tuesday after police intervened at a gathering outside Istanbul’s Caglayan courthouse, where demonstrators had planned to protest about recent detentions targeting LGBTQ+ groups, witnesses said. The detentions marked the latest escalation in what rights groups and opposition figures have described as a widening campaign against the LGBTQ+ community, with authorities over the past week raiding association offices, blocking websites and jailing suspects across multiple provinces. On Tuesday, a group had gathered to make a press statement, but police prevented them from doing so outside the courthouse. Protesters chanted “Long live life in defiance of hate” as police moved in. The protest came after sweeping raids targeting LGBTQ+ associations in several Turkish provinces under an operation dubbed “My Family is Safe,” which the government says is aimed at protecting children and family values. Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Michael O’Flaherty said on Tuesday he was concerned by the arrests, raids and online restrictions targeting LGBTQ+ civil society and human rights defenders. He said references to “family values” or the “protection of children” could not in themselves justify human rights restrictions, and called for the release of anyone detained for human rights or civil society work. A Turkish court on Monday jailed 16 people pending trial in the western province of Izmir as part of the operation, the local prosecutor’s office said. Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said on Sunday the investigations, coordinated by prosecutors in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Aydin and Mersin, involved 162 suspects, nine associations and 13 businesses across 15 provinces. Authorities detained at least 26 people in Istanbul and 21 in Ankara over the weekend and raided the offices of several LGBTQ+ associations. Turkish authorities have also blocked access to websites and social media accounts belonging to various LGBTQ+ associations, individuals and independent media outlets, including the X account of Amnesty International’s Turkey branch.

articles.title: U.S. acknowledges for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space
articles.summary: The United States has confirmed for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The United States has confirmed for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink told the Air and Space Cyber Conference in Maryland on Monday that the U.S. has fielded “on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action.” Meink did not detail what the weapons were or how they work. In 2024 the U.S. said Russia was developing a new anti-satellite weapon that could be launched from space. At the time the White House said the danger wasn’t imminent. But reports of the anti-satellite weapon reflected longstanding worries about space threats from Russia and China, given that much U.S. infrastructure is dependent on satellite communications. In his remarks, Meink also said the Air Force was adding more autonomous systems to its capabilities and predicted the service would look “radically different” by 2032. For example, he foresaw one-way attack drones replacing artillery as the “primary killer.” “We are increasing readiness against existing threats,” he said. President Donald Trump created the Space Force in 2019.

articles.title: Army veteran paratrooper who deployed to Iraq, Afghanistan before helping rescue Fox News reporter dead at 50
articles.summary: Sean Michael Lee's cancer was linked to burn pits in Iraq and Afghanistan, ending a life devoted to rescuing thousands from war zones and disasters.
articles.body: Sean Michael Lee, an Army paratrooper who helped evacuate thousands from conflict zones after his service — including Fox News' Benjamin Hall — died Sunday after a battle with esophageal cancer. Lee was a 20-year veteran of the Army, having served multiple deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan as a member of the Army's storied 82nd Airborne Division, according to his obituary. "He was, to his core, a paratrooper. Long after he took off the uniform, the values forged there remained the organizing principles of his life: duty, loyalty, competence under pressure, and an unwavering commitment to the person beside him," his obituary reads. AMERICA’S PROMISE TO OUR AFGHAN ALLIES IS STILL UNFINISHED FIVE YEARS LATER Lee spent the years after his military service continuing to help people. In 2021, as Afghanistan's government was collapsing, Lee worked to help evacuate thousands during a chaotic withdrawal as a member of the nonprofit group Save Our Allies. Just a year later, Lee was in Poland helping deliver supplies to the frontline in Ukraine in the midst of Russia's invasion. It was there that Lee became a key part of extracting Fox News correspondent Benjamin Hall, who had been severely injured when Russian forces attacked his vehicle near Kyiv. Two members of Hall’s crew were killed in the attack. BENJAMIN HALL TACKLES GRUELING ONE WORLD TRADE CENTER CLIMB ON PROSTHETIC LEGS TO HONOR FALLEN HEROES "We got the call, we had just finished up a staff meeting with our folks back in the United States, and I can tell you that in about 90 minutes our guys were out the door and on the way," Lee explained to the Daily Caller during a 2022 interview. Lee also worked to help wounded veterans through The Independence Fund. In 2024, Lee helped deliver life-saving supplies to survivors of Hurricane Helene in North Carolina. He lived out of a tent in the Tar Heel state as he helped deliver aid to communities where support systems had collapsed, according to his obituary. LUKE COMBS AND ERIC CHURCH RAISE OVER $24.5 MILLION FOR HURRICANE VICTIMS AT STAR-STUDDED CONCERT FOR CAROLINA Most recently, Lee had been working under Secretary Doug Collins at the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. He was part of the U.S. military's 2003 invasion of Iraq. He was also part of the storied Bravo Company in the 2-508 Parachute Infantry Regiment. Half of the company received Purple Hearts for an Afghanistan deployment that was documented in Ben Kesling’s book "Bravo Company: An Afghanistan Deployment and its Aftermath." Lee's two best friends — Sgt. Michael Verardo and Sgt. Allen Thomas — both of whom deployed with him to Afghanistan, passed away before him. Lee's cancer was the direct result of his exposure to the burn pits in Iraq and Afghanistan. He died at age 50. VETERANS FACE SURPRISING THREAT AFTER CANCER DIAGNOSIS, STUDY REVEALS "I can’t even begin to explain what the world has just lost," former MMA fighter and Special Forces sniper Tim Kennedy wrote in a post on Instagram. "This country has lost one of the finest men ever to serve it," Kennedy's message continued. "Sean redefined the word service. He did not just volunteer to put on the uniform and join the 82nd Airborne. He dedicated his entire life to other people. He put his life on the line more times than anyone can count. Wherever people needed help, you found Sean. Whenever I needed help, I found Sean," Kennedy wrote. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Lee's life "cannot be measured simply in years, deployments, jobs, or missions. It is measured in people who made it home because he went toward danger," his obituary, shared by Heritage Funeral & Cremation Services, says. "In wounded men carried to safety. In Afghan families given a chance to begin again. In communities that received help when they believed they had been forgotten. In veterans whose lives were better because he continued serving them after his own time in uniform ended. And in the children who simply knew him as Uncle Sean: the constant, fiercely protective man who showed up." Fox News Digital contacted Save Our Allies for comment.

articles.title: In 1995, Discovery Channel founder John Hendricks bought a Colorado ranch and turned it into a 7,000-acre estate before listing it for $149 million
articles.summary: US News: In the mid-1990s, John Hendricks was already a successful television executive, having built the Discovery Channel into a major documentary and factua.
articles.body: In the mid-1990s, John Hendricks was already a successful television executive, having built the Discovery Channel into a major documentary and factual programming business. In 1995, he bought a ranch in western Colorado, a property far removed from the studios and offices associated with his career. Over the years, the holding expanded into a roughly 7,000-acre estate extending across the Colorado-Utah border. According to the Wall Street Journal, by 2017, when the ranch was put on the market for $149 million, it had developed into something considerably larger than a private country home. There was a 22,000-square-foot main residence, an observatory, an aircraft hangar and thousands of acres set aside under conservation arrangements.John Hendricks turned a Colorado ranch into a 7,000-acre private estateHendricks acquired the Colorado property in 1995, when his career in television was already well established. The Discovery Channel, which he had helped launch in 1985, had grown from a specialist cable network into an international media business centred on factual programming.The ranch offered a very different setting. Located in the red-rock country of western Colorado, close to the Utah state line, it was surrounded by the kind of open landscape that makes conventional measurements of a property feel slightly inadequate.Rather than remaining a relatively modest rural holding, the ranch grew over the following two decades. By the time it was listed for sale, the estate covered about 7,000 acres.That expansion also changed the character of the property. It was no longer simply a large ranch with a substantial house. It had become a private compound designed around the landscape, with buildings and facilities spread across a huge tract of land.A 22,000-square-foot home, private observatory and airplane hangarAt the centre of the estate was a main residence measuring roughly 22,000 square feet. Its size put it in a different category from the traditional ranch houses found across much of the American West.The house was built as a place from which the surrounding landscape could be experienced rather than simply viewed from a distance. The remote setting was an important part of the property, and the scale of the estate meant that privacy came as much from the land itself as from the buildings.There were also facilities that reflected Hendricks' interest in science and exploration. An observatory formed part of the property, giving the estate an unusual feature for a private ranch.An airplane hangar was included as well. On a property of this size and in such a remote location, private aviation provided a practical way of reaching the estate.4,000 acres protected for conservationThe acreage was not all treated as conventional private development land. Around 4,000 acres of the estate had been protected through conservation arrangements.That distinction is significant because the ranch was being marketed not simply on the size of its buildings, but on the amount of open country surrounding them. Conservation restrictions helped preserve portions of the landscape from future development while leaving the property as a very large private holding.The estate's location also gave it a particular physical character. Western Colorado's landscape around the ranch includes exposed rock, canyons and broad stretches of undeveloped terrain. The state border with Utah runs through the wider property, making the ranch unusual geographically as well as in scale.For a buyer, much of the value therefore lay outside the walls of the main residence.The estate and the business of luxury ranchesThe Hendricks property appeared in the Wall Street Journal's coverage of a wider market for high-end ranches and recreational properties.At the time, luxury ranch developments were increasingly being designed around activities such as fly-fishing, with access to productive trout streams becoming part of the sales proposition. Buyers interested in fishing could purchase not just a house and acreage, but a carefully managed outdoor environment.Private fisheries were also becoming part of that market. Some wealthy landowners were spending heavily on stream restoration, fish habitat and water management, bringing biologists and other specialists into what had traditionally been a much simpler part of ranch ownership.Hendricks' ranch belonged to the same broader world of properties where the landscape itself was a major component of the estate.From television headquarters to a remote western retreatThere was an obvious contrast between Hendricks' professional life and the setting of the ranch. His name was closely associated with television documentaries and factual programming. The ranch, by comparison, was built around distance, open land and a comparatively private existence. Its observatory and protected acreage also fitted comfortably with a property designed to make the surrounding environment part of everyday life.The ranch was not in a conventional resort town or suburban luxury market. Its appeal depended heavily on its remoteness.That helped distinguish it from the large estates commonly associated with wealthy buyers in places such as California, New York or Florida. Here, thousands of acres separated the residence from the outside world.Hendricks listed the 7,000-acre ranch for $149 million in 2017According to a local Colorado news report, more than two decades after Hendricks bought the Colorado ranch, the property was placed on the market for $149 million in 2017.The asking price reflected the unusual combination of scale, buildings and protected land. A 7,000-acre estate with a 22,000-square-foot home was already rare. Adding an observatory, an aircraft hangar and thousands of acres under conservation protection made the offering even less conventional.The property was described as straddling the Colorado-Utah border in a region known for its red-rock canyons.By then, what had begun with Hendricks' 1995 purchase had become a vast western estate. The ranch's history was tied not only to the founder of a major television network, but also to a period when wealthy buyers were increasingly treating large working and recreational landscapes as highly specialised luxury properties.The buildings were substantial, but the defining feature remained the land: thousands of acres of western Colorado, with much of it intended to remain open.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Questions swirl over child killer Lucy Letby’s case as UK inquiry reveals major hospital failings
articles.summary: A public inquiry into how the crimes of a British nurse convicted of murdering multiple babies went undetected for so long has uncovered a litany of failings at the UK hospital where she worked and concluded that some babies would have been saved had managers acted sooner.
articles.body: A public inquiry into how the crimes of a British nurse convicted of murdering multiple babies went undetected for so long has uncovered a litany of failings at the UK hospital where she worked and concluded that some babies would have been saved had managers acted sooner. The report found evidence of “dysfunctional management and governance, a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians, and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding” at the hospital where Lucy Letby worked, Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall who chaired the inquiry said Tuesday. “There was also complete failure at all levels to invoke safeguarding procedures at any point,” she added. Letby is serving 15 whole-life sentences for the murders of seven children and attempted murders of seven more between 2015 and 2016, while working at the hospital in Chester, northern England. The case cast Letby as one of Britain’s most prolific child serial killers. But she has always maintained her innocence, and questions about the strength of the evidence her convictions were based on have proliferated since her trial concluded in 2023. Last year an international panel of experts challenged the evidence put forward by the prosecution. The inquiry did not seek to examine Letby’s guilt, focusing instead on whether the Countess of Chester Hospital where she worked could have done more to prevent the deaths. Nonetheless, its findings will likely be used by some of her supporters to bolster the argument that systemic medical failures at the hospital were, at least in part, to blame for the infant deaths. As the fallout from one of the most controversial trials in recent British history continues to spiral more than three years on, here’s what to know: What crimes was Letby convicted of? Letby’s criminal trial in 2023 horrified the nation. The court heard how the former nurse, now 36, attacked babies in her care by administering air into their blood and stomachs, overfeeding them with milk, physically assaulting them and poisoning them with insulin. Justice James Goss described her crimes at the time as a “cruel, calculated and cynical campaign of child murder involving the smallest and most vulnerable of children.” Her crimes and the growing questions over how she was able to escape detection for so long triggered a public inquiry. Part of the investigation’s task was to examine the response of the UK’s National Health Service (NHS), including whether senior staff should have responded differently when suspicions about Letby’s behavior were eventually raised. Thirlwall’s report strongly criticized senior managers and senior nurses for failing to take action when concerns were raised about Letby, while making clear that “some babies would have been saved and some attacks would have been prevented if action was taken earlier.” UK Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said she was “profoundly sorry” for the failures set out in the report, and the harm caused to the victims’ families. She also said training would be urgently reviewed and announced plans for the introduction of “cot cams” in neonatal units. “This must be a turning point for the NHS,” she said. Meanwhile, Jane Tomkinson, the hospital’s CEO, issued an apology and said the institution would address the report’s findings “with openness and a firm commitment to build on the progress we have already made.” Cheshire Police, the principal force involved in Letby’s criminal case, said it would “carefully review” the contents of the report and “fully consider any relevant recommendations.” Why do some think she’s innocent? Letby’s supporters say the prosecution put forward a case based on circumstantial evidence, with a panel of international experts saying in early 2025 that it had found no medical evidence indicating murder. On Monday, Letby’s defense lawyer Mark McDonald said the 14 international experts who made up the panel had come to the same conclusion: the babies Letby was accused of killing died naturally. “I have reports by psychologists on the issue of what was presented to the jury as a confession. It wasn’t a confession at all. I have reports from obstetrics that talk about some of the injuries that were said to have taken place and presented to the jury as an injury, a forceful injury. They weren’t at all,” he told the BBC. Dr. Shoo Lee, a neonatologist who chaired the expert panel, said a research paper he wrote in 1989 was misrepresented in Letby’s trial. “There was no medical evidence to support malfeasance causing death or injury in any of the 17 cases in the trial,” Lee added. The panel’s findings led to a surge of media interest in the UK and around the world questioning the strength of the prosecution’s case. What does the inquiry mean for her convictions? The inquiry has no direct bearing on Letby’s convictions, which have already been tested in the Court of Appeal. However, her defense team has submitted evidence to the UK’s Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), which investigates potential miscarriages of justice, for review. The chair of the CCRC – the only organization with the power to send Letby’s case back to the Court of Appeal after two previous rejections – said the commission would pay close attention to the inquiry’s findings, according to the BBC. Thirlwall said Tuesday, “it’s not for me to second guess or to cut across the work of the Criminal Cases Review Commission, which is working on Letby’s application for her case to be referred back to the Court of Appeal.”

articles.title: Saudi Arabia faces high-stakes choices as war with Houthis escalates
articles.summary: Riyadh has several military options, say analysts, but all of them carry risks, too.
articles.body:
Yemen’s Houthi rebel fighters have broken free from the front lines that have remained broadly frozen in the country since 2022, surging forward to take key positions close to the vital Bab al-Mandeb Strait and opening a new front line in the war that has roiled the region since the US and Israel’s attack on the Houthis’ allies in Iran in February.

In the last few days, Iran-backed Houthi fighters have seized control of the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands and the Red Sea port city of Mocha, tightening the group’s grip on one of the world’s key energy routes in the face of resistance from Yemen’s government-aligned forces.

The Bab al-Mandeb strait’s importance has only grown since Iran, responding to the US and Israeli attacks, proved itself able to significantly restrict shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, with some analysts warning this latest advance stands to add further upward pressure on fuel prices globally.

For Saudi Arabia, the threat is no longer about hypotheticals. A drone strike on its East-West Pipeline, the roughly 1,200km (750-mile) conduit that carries around 4 percent of global oil supplies from the Gulf coast to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, forced a shutdown with future passage unknown.

With that pipeline down and the Houthis tightening their hold on the Red Sea coast and islands near Bab al-Mandeb, Saudi Arabia’s two main alternative export routes around Hormuz risk being squeezed at once.

Through its alliance with the Houthis, Iran is threatening almost a third of the global oil economy, said Baraa Shiban, a researcher and political analyst on Yemen and the Gulf at the Royal United Service Institute (RUSI).

“Iran knew it couldn’t win a traditional battlefront war, so it is inflicting economic warfare on the world,” he said of the US’s inability to sustain a prolonged and expanded conflict in the Gulf. “The last thing Trump can do is go back to the American public and say they need to get engaged on yet another front inside Yemen.”

As the conflict draws closer to Riyadh’s economic lifelines, the relevance of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement , inked between Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan in August, grows more immediate. Earlier this month, Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said the Mecca pact would be activated in the event of an unprovoked attack on Saudi Arabia or if fighting from Yemen were to spill over into the kingdom. “There should be no doubt in this,” Asif said.

However, what shape that intervention might take remains to be seen.

“Saudi Arabia will unfortunately have to find a military option against the Houthis, whether that is limited or long-term,” Shiban said. “In doing so, they will have to test their new agreements,” including both the Mecca pact and its decades-old alliance with Washington.

“They have a long-established relationship with the United States, and I honestly don’t think the US can just watch from a distance,” Shiban continued. “Eventually, the US will have to provide at least logistical, intelligence, and tactical support for Saudi Arabia.”

However, while that might be the case, for now at least, Washington is showing little appetite for taking the fight to the Houthis.

According to reports on the US news site Axios on Friday, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) phoned US President Donald Trump twice the previous day, calling for US military action against the Houthis. On both occasions, the website reported, Trump refused.

Days later, speaking while on a trip to Dublin, Trump told reporters that the Houthis themselves had been in contact, assuring his administration they had no wish to fight US forces. A day later, US Vice President JD Vance confirmed that Washington was in direct talks with the Houthi rebels, as well as its allies in the region, including Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

“It’s probably unhelpful for the US to be speaking directly to the Houthis, and even more unhelpful for the US President to be talking about this on the global stage,” said Elisabeth Kendall, president of Girton College, Cambridge and an authority on Yemeni affairs.

“The Houthis crave political recognition and the international spotlight. Well, now they have it. These kinds of direct talks confer legitimacy. They also throw a spanner in the works of any potential multilateral approach,” she said, referring to previous talks with the Houthis where Oman served as mediator between the US and the rebels.

However, Saudi Arabia is also capable of confronting the Houthi forces directly, analysts point out. The kingdom still fields one of the region’s best-funded air forces and air-defence networks, has backed Yemeni government troops already fighting the Houthis in Taiz , and led a coalition against the group for years before the 2022 truce.

“It is misguided to believe that Saudi Arabia doesn’t have an option for deterrence and retaliation without US support,” Cinzia Bianco of the European Council on Foreign Relations said, adding that this could include calling upon its allies in the Mecca pact, but also acting unilaterally.

“In fact, Riyadh already experienced that US deterrence does not work as well as it did, so they would be looking for creative, asymmetric and hybrid ways to signal deterrence both at the military and political level.”

articles.title: Russia and Ukraine launch new energy attacks despite Trump’s ceasefire claim
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure. Then overnight into Tuesday, both sides launched new energy attacks. Russia fired a volley of 200 drones at Ukraine, hitting energy and port facilities, Ukrainian officials said. In the capital, Kyiv, one person was killed and seven others injured in attacks on two gas stations, warehouses and other sites, according to local authorities. In the south and west, Russian strikes damaged homes, as well as port and transportation infrastructure. Kyiv’s military meanwhile said it struck the Syzran oil refinery in Russia’s Samara region. Ukrainian officials also reported strikes on a drone production facility in Taganrog and a drone preparation and launch site in the Oryol region. This is the daily reality of Russia’s assault, now into its fifth year, to bomb Ukraine’s military and population into submission. The Kremlin has launched near nightly drone and missile attacks on Kyiv and other cities. In an attempt to counter this assault, Ukraine has intensified its campaign of strikes on oil facilities and military targets deep inside Russia. Trump announced Monday that the two sides had agreed to halt this deadly aerial exchange, which Trump said was the primary driver of a global fuel shortage that has seen diesel prices in the United States hit record highs. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seemed to question Trump’s assertion that a deal had bee reached, saying he would only promise to halt energy strikes if Russia did the same, and that he did not trust the Kremlin to do so. The Kremlin welcomed the idea Tuesday but described it as a proposal still being discussed with Washington. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov called Trump’s proposal “a very good idea, a good initiative.” He added that “we are in contact with the Americans. We always support peaceful solutions.” The White House did not immediately respond to request for comment on what exactly had been agreed, and on the apparent disconnect between Trump’s statement and subsequent events. In May, Trump secured a three-day ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine during which time Putin held a “victory day parade.” Earlier this month, both sides agreed to a three-day pause in strikes while Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, held talks in Moscow and Kyiv. These negotiations did not produce demonstrable results and fighting resumed. On Monday, Trump blamed rising diesel prices on the Russia-Ukraine war, including Kyiv’s attempts to repel Russia’s assault, rather than the assault he launched against Iran. That’s despite prices skyrocketing following the American-Israeli bombing campaign on the Islamic Republic, a conflict that shows little sign of ending now into its seventh month. Tuesday also brought developments on the Ukrainian battlefield, with a senior Ukrainian commander announcing a new offensive in Donetsk, near the strategic fortress cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi said his forces had cleared Russian infiltration groups from roughly 29 square miles and recaptured another four square miles. This is a war that also constantly threatens to spill beyond Ukraine’s borders. Overnight into Tuesday, NATO fighter jets shot down an unmanned aircraft in Lithuanian airspace. The drone’s origin remained under investigation. That came less than a day after NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Russian attacks close to the military alliance’s territory would prompt greater support for Ukraine. Separately, Denmark summoned Russia’s ambassador after a Russian warship fired flares toward a Danish military helicopter in the Baltic Sea on Monday, according to Danish authorities.
