articles.title: Henry Zankov is no longer fashion’s best kept secret
articles.summary: New York Fashion Week’s designer of the moment, Henry Zankov, takes us inside his swirling creative universe partly inspired by ’60s French cinema.
articles.body: Every few seasons, New York Fashion Week is in need of a savior. Someone who shakes up what can often be a monotonous cycle of all that goes into the jampacked show calendar. Someone who reminds a likely very jaded and fickle crowd of editors, buyers, and industry observers that fashion can still be thoughtful, genuine, and most importantly, fun. This season, Russian American designer Henry Zankov — the creative auteur behind his namesake label Zankov, and the newly appointed first-ever artistic director of Diane von Furstenberg — feels like that person. Zankov is the definition of the type of personality who has quietly and efficiently “done the work.” Before launching Zankov in 2020, he spent years at New York brands such as Donna Karan and Diane von Furstenberg, as well as consulting for a number of labels under LVMH. In just six short years, his eponymous brand has become a regular go-to for New York’s most clued in — and adventurous — dressers. Known for its knitwear, Zankov’s label embraces unconventional pairings that end up being delightful pieces; think sequin embellished sweaters, color-blocked cardigans, spectacular prints, and endless examples of texture — flowing fringe, peek-a-boo cutouts, scrunched satin, and more. For Zankov, establishing a clear “visual vocabulary” was imperative, even before he fully comprehended what the final line would end up being. “I always really wanted the brand to not be about trends, and really about having a strong visual identity first and foremost. I wanted us to be almost when you see it down the street, or when you see it in the store, or see it on someone else, you automatically know what it is,” Zankov said during an interview in the lead up to New York Fashion Week. “Pattern and color are the two major hallmarks of the brand and its very much rooted in knitwear, but not necessarily only knitwear. I’ve been wanting to grow the collection in a meaningful way, but still everything has to be rooted in color and pattern and incredible materiality with a sense of ease and effortlessness.” Kindred spirits, with a kooky twist The Zankov and Diane von Furstenberg brands have a clear design connection when it comes to playing with prints, pattern and bold color. In a way, the two very different brands –– one an established pillar of New York fashion famed for its ‘70s wrap dress, and the other a respected darling with prime promise — have a sort of big-little sister or kindred spirit association. “There’s definitely similarities. They both very much move through life at their own pace. They’re definitely very much extremely curious and open,” Zankov said. While both brands “share a strong sense of color and a visual vocabulary,” there is one big difference, he added. “I think Zankov is a little bit more freaky. It’s a little bit more subversive and maybe cerebral. And I think DVF is really all about confidence and seduction and effortlessness.” When Zankov first started as artistic director at DVF, he kept thinking, “I’ve got to figure out what the difference is” between the two brands. Now, more than ever, he feels that “the Zankov girl or woman would definitely shop at the new DVF, and vice versa.” The designer’s Spring-Summer 2027 collection saw Zankov dive even deeper into his technicolor universe. Skirts were so heavily encrusted with sequins you could hear them swish over the music on the runway. Oversized spiral print sweaters were paired with chunky platforms. Sheer chiffon cape gowns provided a subtle sex appeal. While his reimagined DVF is sultry and sophisticated, Zankov is refreshingly off-kilter and eccentric. Equal parts cool and kooky. While there’s undoubtedly pressure in reviving a brand as well-known as Diane Von Furstenberg while also continuing to build his own namesake label, it helps that Zankov’s two jobs have two vastly different creative goals and business trajectories. “I think about my friends who love the brand, but can’t really see themselves in it,” he said of bringing a new perspective to DVF. “That’s been my approach — how do we take this and make it desirable to them as well.” Furstenberg’s own personal style remains a creative constant as well, with vintage photos of the designer featured on the studio mood boards. “She is always the ultimate inspiration,” he added. And while the designer dedicates different days to each job, he’s still wearing far more hats while steering Zankov. “Zankov is still so small, so I have to think about production and our development and sales — I don’t get to just design for Zankov, so it’s a little bit more complicated,” he said. “I mean, I just did accounts payable today,” he laughed. Futuristic vision, inspired by the past While crafting his own latest collection, Zankov said he kept turning back to the word “analog” and how that reverberates differently across generations. “I was thinking a lot about my mom in the ‘60s when she moved to St. Petersburg in her 20s, and how that was a time where they went into space and you really felt like the future was around the corner,” said Zankov. “For me, that was in the late ‘90s, early 2000s, when the internet came out, and that also felt like that was the next step of the future.” Zankov also referenced a handful of stills from the 1963 French film, “Bay of Angels.” The story stars actor Jeanne Moreau, and in Zankov’s words is about a woman who “goes to Cannes to gamble her life away.” “It feels very 1960s –– it’s a little bit sexy, but it’s also kooky and weird, but a little sad,” he said of the scenes featuring Moreau that inspired the Zankov show. “It’s vulnerable.” And while Zankov does keep carefully curated mood boards (both for Zankov and DVF) at his dual studio at Furstenberg HQ, his biggest form of inspiration remains simple. “I pull things from everywhere,” he said, pointing to the French word “inspirer” which means to both breathe in and give creative inspiration. “It’s just about being open and keeping your eyes open,” he added. “It starts with a feeling…. but for me, really the inspiration is the work itself — the process, really, going from A to Z.” And now, with two deservedly hyped runway shows behind him, Zankov merely hopes that people — in and out of the industry — continue to see and celebrate the underlying energy that both Zankov and his new vision at DVF share. “It’s about embracing color, embracing a sense of play in the clothes, embracing this idea that not everything has to match. I want clothes to feel easy, and I want everything to feel playful,” he said. Zankov added that he wanted people to feel like they were able to truly play with the clothes, to see themselves wearing items “in their own way, as opposed to everything being a formula, and this is how it is.” “That’s why the whole idea of ease is really important to me,” he added.

articles.title: Russian businessman paid for Trump Jr. wedding after-party: 5 things to know
articles.summary: New reports of Russia-tied financial backing for the after-party events at the May wedding of President Trump’s eldest son have sparked concerns about potential influences from foreign adversaries in the U.S. government ahead of the midterm elections. Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev funded lavish wedding celebrations for Donald Trump Jr. and socialite Bettina Anderson in the…
articles.body:
New reports of Russia-tied financial backing for the after-party events at the May wedding of President Trump’s eldest son have sparked concerns about potential influences from foreign adversaries in the U.S. government ahead of the midterm elections.

Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev funded lavish wedding celebrations for Donald Trump Jr. and socialite Bettina Anderson in the Bahamas, including a private island and a fireworks show, according to a ProPublica investigation published on Monday.

The report raised alarm from Democrats and national security experts about potential ethics violations, as the president and members of his family are typically expected to avoid accepting pricey gifts from adversaries like Russia.

Here are five things to know about this unusual wedding gift:

Kremlev is the head of the International Boxing Association (IBA), a controversy-plagued sports organization financed by Russia’s state-owned natural gas company, Gazprom.

The International Olympic Committee removed IBA from its role organizing boxing events at the global sporting event in 2023, citing the group’s refusal to provide transparent financial information.

Kremlev appealed this decision to Trump in an open letter following his second inauguration last year, expressing the IBA’s interest in seeing the sport represented at the 2028 games in Los Angeles.

“We are very interested in bringing this event back to your country, and we are more than ready to collaborate in this regard,” Kremlev wrote.

The Russian oligarch is a close ally to Russian President Vladimir Putin and traveled with the head of state to China shortly before Trump Jr.’s wedding, according to reports from Chinese state media. In April, Putin presented Kremlev with the Order of Friendship, a high-level state honor.

Additionally, the Ukrainian government has personally sanctioned Kremlev due to his close proximity to the Russian leader.

Kremlev attended Trump Jr.’s 50-person wedding festivities with a group who spoke Russian and “whose presence puzzled other attendees,” ProPublica reported.

Kremlev reportedly covered hundreds of thousands of dollars to fund the cost of Trump Jr.’s after-party events in the Bahamas.

The Russian oligarch rented a private island that has a nightly price tag of $100,000 and a fireworks show from a company that charges around $70,000 per event, according to ProPublica.

He made these payments through a Dubai-based entity affiliated with the IBA.

A spokesperson for Trump Jr. did not deny the wedding payments in a statement to ProPublica, saying that Kremlev was “a personal friend” of the president’s eldest son.

Trump Jr. and his new wife, Bettina Trump, forcefully defended the gift in a statement shared on Instagram amid public criticism.

“Our friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding,” the couple wrote in the post. “It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful.”

Trump did not attend the nuptials or after-party events, citing his executive responsibilities and the Iran war when asked by reporters about his plans ahead of the wedding.

“While I very much wanted to be with my son, Don Jr., and the newest member of the Trump Family, his soon to be wife, Bettina, circumstances pertaining to Government, and my love for the United States of America, do not allow me to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

In a statement shared by the White House with The New York Times on Monday, the president said he had “no idea” who Kremlev was and noted that the Russian oligarch “didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day.”

Democratic lawmakers were quick to condemn this unusual wedding gift from the Russian oligarch.

In a speech from the Senate floor on Monday evening, Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) called it “naked corruption in plain view.”

“This was a Russian party organized and paid for by someone in Vladimir Putin’s inner circle,” Murphy said. “This has never happened before in the history of the United States of America. Never before has a foreign enemy of the United States paid for the family wedding of the president.”

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), the ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee, accused the Trump administration of “Putin-style corruption and authoritarianism” in a Monday social media post .

“When Russian oligarchs pay for American oligarchs’ weddings, it’s a very sweet and romantic gesture, but we know who’s really getting married,” Raskin wrote.

He added, “Let the oligarchs marry — the American people want a divorce of all of them.”

Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.), a member of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, noted previous efforts from Russia to influence U.S. elections.

“Now, we have more evidence that you’ve got a Russian oligarch paying money to a member of the Trump family,” he told MeidasTouch at the Capitol on Monday. “This is very, very scandalous, and we need an explanation from the president and his son.”

Are there rules on these kinds of gifts?

Presidential families are typically expected under ethical norms to not accept expensive gifts from foreign adversaries to avoid the appearance of improper external influences.

While Trump Jr. does not hold an official role in the Trump administration, he has been an influential member during his father’s presidency. In the last presidential election, he successfully advocated for his friend, now-Vice President JD Vance, to be selected as Trump’s running mate.

Russia has a particularly thorny history with attempting to push its political agenda through U.S. officials. The Russian government and Putin have worked to interfere in both the 2016 and 2020 U.S. presidential elections, according to U.S. national security reports.

This gift also came amid the Trump administration’s precarious efforts to broker a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine to end the yearslong conflict. Earlier this month, U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled to both countries to meet with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

articles.title: Armenia is turning westward — the West should take it seriously
articles.summary: For decades one of Russia’s closest allies in the former Soviet Union, the country is preparing to apply for membership in the European Union.
articles.body:
Something remarkable is happening in Armenia. For decades one of Russia’s closest allies in the former Soviet Union, the country is preparing to apply for membership in the European Union.

Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told parliament last month that Armenia intends to submit a formal application “in the near future,” and Moscow’s reaction has already demonstrated how consequential the choice could be.

Russia and its partners in the Eurasian Economic Union have been pressing Armenia to choose between the two blocs. Moscow has warned of economic consequences. Restrictions on Armenian exports to Russia have already become a source of grievance for Armenian farmers.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov responded to Pashinyan’s announcement by warning of “deep trade contradictions that will primarily harm Armenia.” The message is unmistakably clear: Russia has considerable power to make Armenia’s journey to Europe painful.

There is another risk. Armenia could incur the costs of leaving the Russian orbit without ever being securely anchored in the West. It is an old problem for the world’s oldest Christian nation. Armenia has spent much of its history maneuvering between greater powers in search of security, from Rome and Persia to Russia and the West.

Eventually, Russia inherited that role, emerging as the Christian great power capable of challenging Persian and Ottoman domination. That security logic endured into the post-Soviet era. After 1991, Armenia faced Azerbaijan , a closed border with Turkey and no comparable Western security guarantee. In that context, it accepted strategic dependence on Moscow in return for protection.

But then the bargain broke down. The 2020 war with Azerbaijan badly damaged Armenian confidence in Russia. The crises that followed deepened the rupture, culminating in Azerbaijan’s 2023 takeover of Nagorno-Karabakh and the flight of virtually its entire ethnic Armenian population. Russia remained Armenia’s formal ally, but Armenians increasingly concluded that the alliance had failed to provide the protection for which they had sacrificed so much strategic freedom.

It would be easy to interpret what followed as Armenia simply searching for a new protector. But previous geopolitical turns were largely exercises in survival. Today, the shift runs deeper. The West is increasingly where Armenians themselves see their country’s future. Armenia’s technology sector is integrated into global markets. Younger Armenians increasingly look to Europe and the United States for professional, educational and cultural opportunities.

Then there is the diaspora. The U.S. is home to the world’s largest Armenian community outside the former Soviet Union . A deeper U.S.-Armenian relationship could turn that community from an advocate into a conduit for capital, expertise, technology and institutional connections.

That is why Pashinyan’s EU announcement is not simply a European story. Armenia’s movement toward Europe is occurring alongside a potentially transformative relationship with the U.S., most visibly through the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity , or TRIPP.

That U.S.-brokered project envisions a 43-kilometer transit route across southern Armenia connecting Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan and Turkey. It could eventually link Central Asia with Europe while reducing regional dependence on Russia and Iran, while creating opportunities for U.S.-Armenian cooperation in infrastructure, technology, energy and trade.

After a major agreement was reached in June , last month Pashinyan met senior U.S. officials specifically to advance the project, with both sides promising more visible practical steps soon. Negotiations to establish the joint U.S.-Armenian development company are also nearing completion, creating the prospect of sustained American involvement in Armenia’s infrastructure, technology and trade.

TRIPP and EU accession are therefore parts of the same geopolitical story. Europe offers Armenia an institutional destination. The U.S. can offer strategic connectivity, technology and investment, reinforced by an Armenian American community uniquely capable of knitting the two countries together.

If those relationships deepen, Armenia’s Western orientation would cease to depend on the preference of one government or prime minister. It would become rooted in where Armenian companies do business, where investment comes from and how the country connects to the world.

This does not mean Armenia is simply exchanging Moscow for Washington. It wants consequential relationships with Europe and the U.S., but also with China, India, Iran and others.

For a country whose history has repeatedly left it dependent on a single external protector, diversification is itself a form of sovereignty. EU membership, however, would be different in kind. It would eventually place Armenia inside a Western political, economic and institutional system. Combined with an expanding American relationship, it would amount to a genuine geopolitical realignment.

Armenia has attempted a Western turn during a period of Russian weakness before. When the Russian Empire collapsed in 1917, independent Armenia similarly looked West. Woodrow Wilson became the symbol of Armenian hopes for an external guarantee, but Western sympathy never became enforceable protection. In the aftermath of the Armenian Genocide, caught between Turkish forces and Bolshevik Russia, the First Republic disappeared in 1920.

A century later, Armenians are taking another chance. The West has an opportunity to do it right this time.

Grigor Hovhannissian is a former Armenian ambassador to the United States and Mexico and a former deputy foreign minister of Armenia.

articles.title: Trump and Xi Jinping summit to highlight U.S.-China AI competition and national security risks
articles.summary: The United States and China are both gripped by safety fears as they reckon with their rapid advances in AI, but intensifying competition and deep mutual distrust could derail the kind of cooperation experts say is vital to head off the strategically vital technology’s greatest dangers.
articles.body: BEIJING — The United States and China are both gripped by safety fears as they reckon with their rapid advances in AI, but intensifying competition and deep mutual distrust could derail the kind of cooperation experts say is vital to head off the strategically vital technology’s greatest dangers. Artificial intelligence is increasingly at the center of the rivalry between Washington and Beijing, and is expected to be a major topic of discussion at a summit in Washington next week between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. The summit comes as AI leaders and researchers in the U.S. warn that companies should “slow the pace” of AI development, citing recent incidents involving autonomous agents. Trump has dismissed such concerns as a “hoax” while agreeing with executives such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that the U.S. must maintain AI dominance over China through export controls and other measures. China, which tightly regulates AI and largely avoids the existential worries the technology provokes in the U.S., has interpreted calls to slow its development as targeted squarely at its own progress. U.S. companies say the Chinese AI sector is being driven in part by large-scale “illicit distillation” of their most advanced models. Chinese officials, who say distillation is a conventional practice that U.S. companies also use on Chinese models, in turn accuse America’s AI executives of trying to stave off competition. Senior Col. Zhu Qichao, a noted voice on Chinese military AI and national security, called for “cooperation” with the U.S. while warning against “vicious competition.” “Because with the development of emerging technologies, it definitely comes with many possibilities,” said Zhu, the director of the Institute for Defense Technology and Strategic Studies at the People’s Liberation Army National University of Defense Technology. “On one hand, it benefits humanity, but on the other hand, there are also considerations regarding risks,” he told NBC News on Tuesday at the Xiangshan Forum in Beijing. AI and the worries around it were a major focus at the annual defense forum, where rooms were packed with scholars, military officials and commentators from the U.S. and other countries, many of which are being pressured to pick sides in the U.S.-China AI race. Though Trump and Xi agreed at their May summit in Beijing to hold high-level AI talks, no such talks have been publicly confirmed ahead of Xi’s visit next week. Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, said China was wary that the talks could be used to further slow its progress. “On the other hand, I think both sides need to sit down to talk about the risks posed by AI development,” he said at the forum, adding that “it will take a long way before the two sides can really forge some important consensus on this issue.” For U.S.-China cooperation to work, the U.S. needs to be open to both sides benefiting, said Francesca Giovannini, executive director of the Harvard Belfer Center’s Initiative on Managing the Atom. “The United States operates on a very specific type of theory. And the theory is, whoever wins the AI race wins everything,” she said in an interview at the forum. “So if this is your zero-sum game idea, you won’t be conceding anything.” China is unlikely to agree to a slowdown at the behest of U.S. AI companies, said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at the Asia Group, an American strategic advisory firm based in Washington. “I don’t think what happens in the U.S. really matters to China,” he said Tuesday in a phone interview from Hong Kong. “They want to do AI at their own pace, and to a very large degree a lot of people in the industry, in the government, they have a very proud sense that this is finally the chance for China.” China, which sees its “open-weight” AI models as a tool for diplomacy, has promoted the technology as a global “public good” that should be managed by the international community. At a summit in India on Sunday, Xi offered the 11-member BRICS group of nations help developing open-source AI and urged them to join China’s global AI governance initiative. But China is also keenly aware of the risks it faces from its own AI success, with Xi telling a Shanghai conference in July that authorities must “ensure that AI is always under human control.” The industry must make mandatory filings and submit security assessments to officials, with many of the companies having to submit technical filings to an algorithm registry. The government has also imposed rules requiring watermarking and safety requirements. Foremost among the risks are potential threats to China’s ruling Communist Party, which worries the technology could be weaponized against it and has imposed ideological controls to ensure products fall in line with socialist values, for example. “Hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives misuse generative AI technologies — such as deepfake audio-video, AI-generated graphics and text, and intelligent bot farms — to manufacture political rumors, spread harmful information, and incite confrontation at low cost and on a massive scale,” Chen Yixin, the Chinese minister of state security, said in an article Sunday in the state-backed China Cybersecurity Magazine that called for greater party control and government oversight of AI. Chen said AI could enable misinformation campaigns and cyberattacks on China’s critical infrastructure and, in an apparent reference to the U.S., warned that countries with “advantages” in AI could restrict other nations’ access to their technologies. He also warned of espionage and data leaks, days after Anthropic released a report that found Chinese AI labs had secretly routed requests to its Claude models, some of which contained sensitive information from individuals, major companies and state-affiliated actors. Like the U.S., China increasingly views AI as a national security issue, down to the individual researchers working on it. On Tuesday, China tightened travel curbs on its citizens, barring some whose work has implications for national technology security from leaving the country. The new rules add to an extensive AI regulatory regime that includes restrictions on AI companions over mental health concerns, mandated labeling of AI-generated content and a requirement that trained models must use data conforming to Chinese values. Experts say it could take a major crisis for the U.S. and China to finally work together on AI, much like the 1962 Cuban missile crisis pushed the U.S. and the then-Soviet Union to start negotiating on nuclear weapons. AI has already had profound military implications, including for targeting, and could be integrated into systems supporting the nuclear chain of command, said David Finkelstein, vice president of the Center for Naval Analyses. “This is scary stuff, and I think that this is an area where the two sides ought to be sitting down and talking to each other,” he said at the forum. U.S.-China competition is inevitable, but there is still room for the two sides to negotiate because their respective positions “are not necessarily very much entrenched,” said David Santoro, president and chief executive of Pacific Forum International, a Honolulu-based think tank. “There are still ways that we can better understand each other and hopefully come up with mechanisms so we can better control this emerging technology,” he said in an interview at the forum. Santoro said he was “not very optimistic,” however, about the prospect for a major agreement in the near term. “I don’t know that we will be able to get to a position where we agree on something substantive,” he said. “But at least the first step has got to be talking to each other.” Eric Baculinao and Erin Tan reported from Beijing, and Mithil Aggarwal from Hong Kong.

articles.title: Kenya planted Grevillea trees among maize to make farms more productive; long-term research found their roots competed for the same soil water
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Farmers across Kenya have long planted Grevillea trees alongside maize, hoping the tall, fast-growing species would add timber, shade and income witho.
articles.body: Farmers across Kenya have long planted Grevillea trees alongside maize, hoping the tall, fast-growing species would add timber, shade and income without hurting the crop underneath. A long-term field trial in semi-arid Kenya put that idea to the test over 4.5 years and nine growing seasons, tracking maize and cowpea grown either alone or alongside grevillea trees. The findings come from a study called Long-term productivity of a Grevillea robusta-based overstorey agroforestry system in semi-arid Kenya: II. Crop growth and system performance, published in the journal Forest Ecology and Management, based on a trial at Machakos in eastern Kenya. For the first four seasons, crop yields in the tree and maize plots matched those grown without trees. But as the grevillea matured, yields collapsed in most later seasons, falling close to zero in three of the final four, and reaching as much as half the tree-free yield only in the one season when rainfall was unusually high, pointing to a problem hiding underground rather than up in the canopy.How researchers separated the effects of shade from competition for waterThe experiment, known as the CIRUS trial, was established at the ICRAF Machakos Research Station in Kenya. Grevillea trees were planted in a dispersed arrangement either as sole stands or alongside crops. Cowpea and maize were rotated during the first five seasons after the trees were planted, while maize was grown continuously during the final four seasons. One growing season was lost when the rains failed. To determine how much of the crop decline could be explained simply by reduced sunlight, the researchers also grew sole maize beneath shade netting that reduced incoming radiation by 25%, 50% or 75%. The comparison produced an important result. Maize growing alongside the trees performed worse than maize grown under the artificial shade treatments. If reduced sunlight had been the main reason for the yield losses, heavily shaded maize should have performed similarly to the maize growing beneath grevillea. Instead, the shade-net crops generally produced more biomass and grain. The researchers therefore concluded that shading alone could not explain the decline and that below-ground competition for resources, particularly water, was becoming increasingly important as the trees matured.Why grevillea roots ended up competing with maize below groundA companion study at the same Machakos site examined the roots of grevillea and maize directly. Root samples showed that the two species were not neatly separated into different soil layers. The maximum root length densities of both species occurred in the upper soil layer, while grevillea dominated the root population at different depths. When maize was grown with the trees, its root growth into deeper soil was also suppressed. The researchers concluded that severe competition for water should be expected unless the trees had access to a separate source of water unavailable to the crop. That finding challenged the assumption that grevillea would avoid competing heavily with maize simply because trees can make use of deeper soil water. The tree-growth study from the same experiment found that grevillea continued growing through the dry season, sometimes at rates comparable to or greater than those recorded during cropping seasons, suggesting that the trees could make use of residual soil moisture or deeper reserves. As the trees became the dominant component of the system, the balance between the tree and crop shifted increasingly in their favour.What happened to maize yields as the grevillea trees maturedThe change was gradual rather than immediate. During the first four seasons, maize and cowpea grown with grevillea were not significantly different from the corresponding sole crops. But the performance of the understorey crops declined sharply during later seasons as the trees became more dominant. The study reports that performance ratios for the crops, which compare their output with sole-crop stands, approached zero during three of the final four seasons. By contrast, the trees' performance relative to sole grevillea stands increased as they established. Rainfall could still change the severity of the competition. Maize reached half the yield of the corresponding sole crop only once during the final four seasons, when rainfall was unusually high. In another study of crop performance at the site, maize biomass approached half that of sole maize after above-average rainfall, while grain yield was still only 36% of the sole-crop value. This shows why the effect was particularly important in a semi-arid environment: when water was plentiful, the crop could partly recover, but when water was limited, competition with established trees became much harder to overcome.What the Kenya experiment means for tree-and-crop agroforestryThe experiment does not show that grevillea and maize can never be grown together. Instead, it shows that the balance between the two can change dramatically as the trees mature. During the early years, the crops and trees could coexist without a significant reduction in maize or cowpea yield. Later, the growing grevillea canopy and, more importantly, its extensive root system increased competition for resources. The researchers concluded that the viability of the system depended on understanding these changing interactions rather than assuming that the benefits of agroforestry would remain constant as the trees grew. For semi-arid farming systems, the finding is particularly relevant because water availability can determine whether competition remains manageable or becomes severe. The Machakos experiment shows that a tree that appears compatible with a crop during its first few years may become a much stronger competitor as its root system and biomass develop. In this case, the problem was not simply that grevillea blocked sunlight from reaching maize. Much of the competition was happening underground, where the roots of both species were drawing on overlapping parts of the soil profile.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: Policy change sparks heated Senate debate; critics question its timing amid challenges in attracting new FBI agents.
articles.body:
United States FBI Director Kash Patel has defended the bureau’s loosening of hiring requirements regarding prostitution and bestiality, saying the changes were meant to enable victims of those acts to apply for employment without fear of automatic disqualification.

The FBI quietly issued guidance this past spring lifting a categorical hiring ban on applicants who had previously engaged in prostitution, and said that it would instead consider the context of the behaviour in at least some cases. The bureau made a similar change regarding bestiality.

Pressed about the moves at a Senate Judiciary Committee oversight hearing, Patel on Tuesday denied that the changes reflected a lowering of employment standards and insisted they were designed to protect victims forced to engage in that conduct and to prevent automatic disqualification.

“We did not want to punish victims of bestiality, victims who were trafficked. We did not want to make it an automatic disqualification for the FBI to consider you,” Patel said.

The answer did little to satisfy Republican Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana, who grilled Patel on the rationale for a change the FBI director said subordinates proposed to him.

Kennedy asked Patel why, given the FBI’s current difficulty attracting new agents because of negative public sentiment, Patel would make these changes now.

“Why would you even get into bestiality?” Kennedy said.

Patel replied it was a way of supporting victims, and that some people who were “forced into” bestiality should not be disqualified.

The Republican-led panel tried to keep the focus on Patel’s efforts to combat violent crime, counter drug trafficking and pursue the Trump administration’s agenda from his perch at the nation’s premier federal law enforcement agency.

But Democrats seized on the tumult inside the FBI over the last year, including sweeping firings of agents who participated in investigations into President Donald Trump, the bureau’s efforts to investigate Trump’s perceived political adversaries and Patel’s travel schedule, which has blended private leisure with professional responsibilities.

“Mr Patel is the least qualified and most partisan FBI director in our nation’s history,” Senator Dick Durbin of Illinois, the panel’s top Democrat, said in his opening statement at the hearing. He accused Patel of wielding the bureau’s law enforcement powers to seek retribution against Trump’s political opponents and pursue the president’s grievances, including his false claims that the 2020 election he lost was stolen.

Patel has made multiple appearances before Congress while serving as director, including to testify about the FBI’s budget, but this was his first time since last September before the Senate committee that has primary oversight jurisdiction over the bureau.

That hearing featured feisty and personal exchanges with Democrats, with Patel at one point shouting over Senator Adam Schiff of California, calling him an “utter disgrace” and a “coward”.

“You can make an internet troll the FBI director, but he will always be an internet troll,” Schiff shot back.

Tuesday’s hearing was expected to be no less contentious given Democrats’ fierce criticism of his leadership and conduct. Durbin called for Patel to be replaced as director in April following an article by The Atlantic magazine that raised allegations of excessive drinking.

Patel later filed a $250 million defamation lawsuit, calling the article false and a “malicious hit piece”. The Atlantic said it stood by its reporting and would vigorously defend against the “meritless lawsuit”.

articles.title: Election in Philippines’ Bangsamoro region ends in hung parliament
articles.summary: No party wins majority in parliamentary polls in southern Philippines’ Muslim-majority region, unofficial results show.
articles.body:
Marawi City, Philippines – The first parliamentary election in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in the southern Philippines has resulted in a hung parliament as no single party managed to secure a majority, according to unofficial results.

With more than 99 percent of votes counted as of Tuesday evening, the two rival parties that emerged from the separatist Moro Islamic Liberation Front each had more than 30 percent of the vote, showed the partial count of GMA News, one of the country’s largest news networks. Neither secured the 41 seats needed for a majority in the 80-member parliament.

The front signed a peace agreement with the Philippine government in 2014 after decades of conflict for independence and self-governance. It served as an interim government after voters approved the autonomous region in 2019. But last year, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr replaced longtime Moro Islamic Liberation Front chairman Al Haj Murad Ebrahim with Abdulraof Macacua, a former front commander, as chief minister, in a move that worsened internal divisions in the Muslim-majority region.

Macacua, who leads the Bangsamoro Federalist Party, has acknowledged that a coalition with other parties is “an unavoidable situation” following Monday’s vote.

Ebrahim told reporters after casting his ballot that he hoped his party – the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) – would clinch most of the seats, but expressed openness to negotiating with other parties.

“If the party does not get majority of the seats, we will look for parties who can be our allies so that we can form a coalition,” Murad said.

Some voters had feared a return to fighting if the UBJP failed to get a commanding lead, especially because the front has halted the disarming of former fighters, citing the government’s failure to provide aid as promised.

“One of the commanders of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front has said that if they don’t win the election, there might be war again,” Alinair Aracaya said.

The commander he was referring to was 64-year-old Abdullah Macapaar – also known as Commander Bravo and notorious for being one of the most defiant front leaders. On Monday, Macapaar, who was also running to become a member of parliament, voted for the first time in his life.

In a Facebook post, Miriam Coronel-Ferrer, who led peace negotiations with the front on behalf of the government, commended the participating parties “for their great effort to build their capacity to enter the field of electoral politics and play by the rules of the electoral process”.

Authorities said the elections were generally peaceful, but security forces will remain on high alert in the coming days. Multiple shooting incidents on election day left at least three people dead and several wounded.

“We will still hold our deployment in place even after the proclamation of winners. We are trying to ensure that the security situation will remain stable,” said Brigadier General Jemuel Siason, deputy police director of the Bangsamoro region.

After years of negotiations, the Philippine government and Moro Islamic Liberation Front signed a peace agreement that paved the way for autonomy in the region.

Voter Aracaya’s wife, Norhailyn Madayan, remembers a childhood spent fleeing conflict. “Just the sight of soldiers terrified us because that meant there might be clashes again. There were also clan wars,” Madayan said.

Aracaya and Madayan said peace has allowed them to build a life. They have a thriving business and a newly constructed concrete home. But they also say peace has been fragile. In 2016, ISIL-linked fighters briefly took control of their town.

The following year, the same group laid siege to Marawi City. The military responded with air attacks.

Asraf Balt, a resident, was only nine years old at the time. But because shots rang out every now and then, he said he did not immediately realise the gravity of the situation until he saw what happened to their home.

“We got displaced, and our house got destroyed. Like, heavily destroyed to the point that we had to rebuild it,” Balt said. His family has moved back to their home, but hundreds of others remain in temporary shelters.

Analyn Pangandaman said her family cannot afford to rebuild their home without reparation from the government. She has been waiting to get compensated for nearly nine years.

Now, she says, she cannot even visit her mother, even if she lives just a few towns away.

“I used to see my parents a lot, but I don’t any more because I can’t afford the commute. We used to be able to visit them because we had a car,” Pangandaman said.

With the Bangsamoro region having been able to conclude its first election, Pangandaman hopes to receive what the government owes her family soon. And it’s only possible, she says, if winning parties set aside differences and work together towards peace and progress.

articles.title: Introducing OutKick's first original animated series, 'Sports Talk with Cal McCallister'
articles.summary: "Sports Talk with Cal McCallister" is OutKick's first original animated series featuring a doddering radio legend and his producer/grandson.
articles.body: A lot of really exciting stuff has been happening here at OutKick over the last few weeks. We’ve got Craig Carton coming on board with a show, and a bunch of new features like OutKick Outdoors, OutKick Dropkick, and OutKick University getting up and running and hitting their stride. So it’s a great time to introduce you to OutKick’s first original animated series, "Sports Talk with Cal McCallister." Take a look at the trailer (which features narration from the great Dan Dakich): We’ve got a batch of animated shorts that you’ll be able to see over the next couple of months, featuring Cal McCallister, a radio legend and doddering old curmudgeon with decades of experience on the airwaves. He has plenty of hot takes to dish out, but winds up spending most of his time mixing it up with his callers and trying to keep his show on the rails with the help of his producer/grandson, Jody. The first of these will debut Wednesday on the OutKick YouTube channel and on social media. Yes, like tomorrow. That Wednesday. There will be eight of these episodes, and I’m proud to say that each one was made the old-fashioned way: me sitting at my desk, drawing on my wife’s old iPad that I commandeered (with her permission). See? Just the way Tex Avery used to do it… Don’t fact-check that. Countless hours since last December were spent writing scripts, doing voices, writing and composing pieces of original music, editing, and, of course, animating. While I was a one-man shorts-producing operation (albeit a very smart and handsome one), I couldn’t truly get the job done alone. I got some big help behind the scenes to get this all ready for release, and you’ll also hear some familiar OutKick voices. I hope you enjoy watching them as much as we did making them. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER So, be sure to catch new episodes of "Sports Talk with Cal McCallister" every Wednesday and follow Cal, @SportsTalkCal, on X and Instagram.

articles.title: Letby failings go beyond one hospital - the whole NHS system has been found lacking
articles.summary: Inquiry chair Lady Justice Thirlwall set out how the culture of the health system created the conditions that enabled poor care and criminality.
articles.body:
The public inquiry into the Lucy Letby case may have reserved the strongest criticism for the Countess of Chester Hospital and its management, but there are big questions for the wider NHS to answer too.

The Thirlwall inquiry's final report said there was a "complete failure" to protect babies on the neonatal unit where Letby murdered seven and attempted to murder seven more.

But a third of the report was given over to the wider role played by the health system in England - and make no mistake, it was found lacking.

Across more than 200 pages, inquiry chair Lady Justice Thirlwall set out how the culture of the health system created the conditions that enable poor care - or in this case criminality - to go unchecked for so long.

The failures encompass everything from regulation and employment practices to the way the NHS and government struggle to learn the lessons of the past.

They have prompted Health Secretary Yvette Cooper to say she "will not hesitate" to hold the system to account at every level.

She has promised to set up a hub to track the progress on implementing the inquiry's recommendations and pointed to the creation of a new maternity and neonatal commissioner post as a sign of her commitment to improving standards.

"This must be a turning point for the NHS," she told the House of Commons when responding to the publication of the report. So what needs to change?

The inquiry said NHS managers have become pre-occupied with avoiding blame, leading to an "over-focus on process and reputation management".

One witness described this as "blame engineering", with the inquiry concluding this was a key characteristic in the way Countess of Chester bosses approached the Letby case with the report describing it at one point as an "exercise in spin".

This approach to management means raising the alarm becomes difficult - a concern that has been repeated again and again in inquiries into other scandals.

There have been plenty of initiatives to address this over the years. In the last decade, this has taken the form of the Freedom to Speak Up programme with each NHS organisation having a "guardian" whose job is it to support staff who want to issue a concern.

But in a number of places the initiative has become a "box ticking" exercise

The result? A "toxic negativity" persists around whistleblowing with staff discouraged from speaking out, the inquiry said.

This view is supported by the NHS staff survey which showed a declining confidence in speaking out.

The donkey sanctuary for failing managers

There is, the Thirlwall inquiry said, a consistent inability within the NHS to deal with poor performance.

Failing managers will be moved, often with the active assistance of NHS England, in a process referred to as rehabilitation, the inquiry heard.

Countess of Chester chief executive Tony Chambers referred to it as "the donkey sanctuary".

The report even noted how some failing managers receive pay offs and move on elsewhere "with few questions asked" as NHS trusts worry about the threat of employment tribunals.

While there are many excellent managers in the NHS, profound change is needed in the way the NHS deals with those who fail, the inquiry added.

The government wants to bring in a barring service, but the inquiry warned this will be undermined if the system continues to turn a blind eye like it does.

Key findings from Lucy Letby Thirlwall Inquiry

Regulators not asking the right questions

Regulation has also been found lacking. The Care Quality Commission (CQC) inspected the Countess of Chester in February 2016 - Letby carried on attacking babies until June of that year.

Key information was withheld from inspectors, but the regulator was criticised for not showing enough curiosity to look beyond what they were being told.

Only a year before, the CQC had been warned by another inquiry into baby deaths at Morecambe Bay NHS Trust that it needed to take a tougher approach.

Weaknesses have persisted since, the Thirwall inquiry said. An independent review in 2024 warned the ability of the CQC to spot poor performance was by that point deteriorating.

The CQC has released a statement acknowledging it was not investigative or inquiring enough in 2016, but said it had since strengthened its approach.

Meanwhile, the Nursing and Midwifey Council, which regulates nurses, was also told it should have been more curious - it renewed Letby's registration at a time when she was not permitted to work on a ward and a police investigation was taking place.

Lessons of previous scandals not being learned

As part of its work, the inquiry looked at why the lessons of previous inquiries have not been learned.

There has been countless inquiries dating back 30 years, with thousands of recommendations made.

But the Thirwall inquiry said most of these have not been implemented - and, when they have, it has taken too long or progress has not been tracked.

It blamed, among other things, a lack of political will and disruption caused by repeated structural reorganisations.

This had a potentially significant impact in the Letby case, the inquiry suggested. It cited the medical examiner system, whereby an independent doctor looks into deaths that are not reviewed by a coroner so that the cause of death is not down to the doctor involved in the patients care to sign off.

The move was recommended in 2003 by the inquiry into the Harold Shipman murders and called for again a decade later as part of the inquiry into the failings at Mid Staffordshire NHS Trust. But it took until 2024 for it to be introduced.

Former health secretary Sir Jeremy Hunt told the inquiry he believes it would have prevented a number of deaths at the Countess of Chester if it had been in place sooner.

articles.title: Why Trump’s diesel woes are playing right into Moscow’s hands
articles.summary: Faced with record diesel prices and less than two months to go until the midterm elections, Donald Trump has reverted to a default setting in his turbulent and abortive campaign to end the Ukraine war: blaming the victim. His timing could not be worse for Ukraine, or more beneficial to Russia.
articles.body: Faced with record diesel prices and less than two months to go until the midterm elections, Donald Trump has reverted to a default setting in his turbulent and abortive campaign to end the Ukraine war: blaming the victim. His timing could not be worse for Ukraine, or more beneficial to Russia. “Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing: He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” the US president told reporters Sunday, referring to his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky. “It’s hurting the world.” Trump’s attitude is at best inconsistent, coming less than a year after sources told CNN the US had increased intelligence-sharing with Ukraine so it could hit Russian energy sites (back when oil prices were low), and barely a week after he claimed gas prices would come down when the Iran war ends (without mentioning the Ukraine war). It’s also incorrect, according to analysts, to claim that if Ukraine stopped attacking Russian refineries, the price problem would be solved. Andy Lipow, from Texas-based Lipow Oil Associates, estimates that Russia’s decision to ban exports in response to Ukrainian attacks has taken 800,000 barrels per day of diesel off the market. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, meanwhile, has affected 1.2 million barrels a day. At worst, this is another betrayal of Kyiv, which, faced with a critical lack of air defenses, is playing one of the few cards it has left — hitting Russia’s military machine and the energy resources that power it on Russian soil. The betrayal is all the more painful, coming amid almost constant Russian drone and missile attacks and ahead of a winter that Moscow openly plans to weaponize. On Monday, Trump claimed on Truth Social that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on each other’s energy sites (spoiler: they hadn’t). What followed in the Kremlin’s response was a master class in truth-twisting, as it extracted every last drop of PR gold. First, simple tactics. In a comment likely designed to placate Trump, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the proposal “a very good idea,” adding: “We are in contact with the American side.” He also offered up the usual fiction designed to make Ukraine look bad: “We always favor peaceful solutions.” Then, a more delicate maneuver: how to continue painting Ukraine as the aggressor without letting slip the facade that the refinery strikes are not actually that bad for Russia. “While such a truce would allow us to fully saturate our domestic market… it is currently nearing full saturation,” Peskov claimed. “The issue is not production; it is about ensuring unhindered access for these petroleum products to global markets.” That allowed him to deflect from refineries to a recent surge in Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil tankers. No mention of Russia’s attacks on commercial shipping and Ukrainian ports. And then the final salvo from Peskov: “The second necessary step is, of course, to lift the sanctions. Only then will the world be adequately supplied with these petroleum products.” The Kremlin may see an opening here. The US temporarily lifted some sanctions on Russia earlier this year as the Iran war threatened oil supplies. It could also be an attempt to avert the opposite outcome. This week, the Trump administration slapped sanctions on one of Russia’s biggest banks over its ties to Iran, at the same time as the US House moved closer to a vote on a sweeping Russian sanctions bill co-authored by Sen. Lindsey Graham before his death in July. For Zelensky, this must feel like whiplash. It was just over a week ago that Trump’s foreign policy envoys hugged him, cameras flashing, in the middle of Kyiv on their long-promised first trip to Ukraine, offering up hope of new momentum for diplomacy. The warning signs were there. They had gone to Russia first. Trump followed up with a call to Putin, but not Zelensky. And while Patriot interceptor supplies are still on the table, Trump remarked this week they were considering “a less sophisticated version” for Kyiv. Even if you strip out Trump’s apparent personal preference for Putin and the factual inconsistencies in his decision to blame Ukraine for diesel prices, we’re back to the central debate that has shaped this conflict from the start. How to punish Russia, a systemically important oil producer, without punishing yourself in the process? And will any resolve to do so go out the window when oil prices rise?
